title: Listening in conversation
hookLine: the Japji's power of listening, in conversation
tomorrow: simran owes kiran a sorry. why is 'sorry, but' so tempting?

cards: Kiran calls after school, and Simran is ready. She has advice. Talk to the coach.
Post something chill. Come back to lunch, I'll save you a seat. Kiran starts to say something, and Simran talks over her, kindly, three times.
Then a long pause on the line. Kiran says, quietly: my mom had surgery. I've been home with my little brother.
That's where I've been. All the advice goes quiet. Simran never let her get that far.

teach.b: The Japji has a run of pauris that each begin with one word: suniai, by listening. By listening, Guru Nanak says, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away; by listening, the devotees bloom.
Now the debate, and it's a real one among Sikhs who love these lines. One side says: careful.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: IT MEANS HEARING THE NAME.
teach.b: In the Japji, listening means hearing the Name, the Word, Gurbani itself. It's the soul hearing the Divine, not a tip for phone calls, and stretching it that far can shrink it.

teach.h: THE OTHER: THE LIGHT IS IN EVERYONE.
teach.b: The other side says: Gurbani also says the one light is in everyone. If that's true, listening to a person is never only small talk. Hearing Kiran out is part of hearing the One who lives in her.
Each side keeps something worth keeping. The first keeps the Japji from becoming a self-help card. The second keeps it from staying on the page.
Some Sikhs hold both: the deep listening of the Japji trains the ear, and the ear goes with you into every conversation. So Simran tries it.
She says, sorry, I talked over you. Tell me about your mom. Then the hard part.
She doesn't say anything else for a long time.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji, including its pauris on listening, in the morning; some also speak of listening to Gurbani in the sangat as practice for listening to people.

o: hearing someone out fully before you answer
nodding along while you plan what to say
staying silent so nobody can blame you

p: the one light is in everyone

s: the Japji's listening pauris are mainly advice about conversations
they're first about hearing the Name; applying them to people is a reading some hold alongside.
in the Japji, by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away
that's the promise of the suniai pauris.

games.q: your uncle says the Japji's listening is about Gurbani, not about being a good listener at dinner. what's his side's best case?
o: suniai is the soul hearing the Name; turning it into manners shrinks it.
the Japji never mentions listening; that idea came later from teachers.
in Sikh teaching only scripture deserves listening, not people.
games.why: in the Japji, by listening points first to the Name and the Word. the other side adds that the one light is in everyone. some Sikhs hold both.

practice: Choose one sound around you: traffic, a fan, birds, someone in the next room. Give it your whole attention, the way you'd want to be heard, and when your mind starts drafting a reply to it, notice that and come back.
Stay with the sound as the sit begins.

wordCard.voice: Listening in conversation. Hearing someone all the way to the end, the way suniai asks the ear to hear.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suniai, by listening; the word that opens a run of the Japji's pauris.

carryVoice: Your line: listen fully. Advice can wait until the whole story is done. Talk soon.

sources.ref: Ang 13 (Sohila, Dhanasri, Mahala 1: sabh meh jot jot hai soe), paraphrased
